meta.title_plain: Why winning 55% of points wins most matches
meta.teaser: A tiny edge on each point grows into a huge edge in the match.

page.title: Why winning 55% of points wins most matches
page.bigIdea: Tennis scoring stacks points into games, games into sets and sets into matches. Each layer turns a small edge into a big one.

cards.title: Tennis is a ladder
cards.front: Why don't you just count total points?
cards.back: Points build games, games build sets, and sets build the match. You need 4 points for a game and 6 games for a set, winning by 2.
cards.tryit: Watch one set on TV or YouTube. Count how many points each player wins. Did the winner always win more?

cards.title: A tiny edge per point
cards.front: What does winning 55% of points feel like?
cards.back: Picture a coin that lands heads 11 times in every 20 flips. That's 55%. It's only a little better than a fair coin, and you lose almost half the time.
cards.tryit: Flip a coin 20 times and count heads. Do it twice. Notice how much the count jumps around.

cards.title: The edge grows each level
cards.back: In a simple maths model, winning 55% of points means winning about 62% of games, 82% of sets and 91% of best-of-three matches.
cards.tryit: Draw a ladder with four rungs: point, game, set, match. Write each percentage on its rung.

cards.title: Federer's 54% secret
cards.front: Even the greats lose lots of points.
cards.back: Roger Federer won about 80% of his 1,526 singles matches, but only 54% of his points. He said, "In tennis, perfection is impossible."
cards.tryit: In your next practice, after a lost point, take one breath and let it go before the next one.

cards.title: Your challenge
cards.front: At deuce, you win each point 60% of the time. What's your chance of winning the game?
cards.back: Win two in a row: 0.6 × 0.6 = 36%. Lose two: 0.4 × 0.4 = 16%. Otherwise it's deuce again. So you win 36 out of 52, about 69%.
cards.tryit: Redo the deuce puzzle with 50%. Does your answer make sense? Then try 55%.

quiz.q: You win each point 60% of the time. What's your chance of winning the next two points?
quiz.hint: Can a chance ever be bigger than 100%? Think about multiplying.
quiz.why: Both must happen, so you multiply: 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36, which is 36%.

quiz.q: Two players each win exactly 50% of points. What's the first player's chance of winning the match?
quiz.hint: Try swapping the two players' names. Does anything change?
quiz.why: The players are perfectly equal, so the scoring can't favour either one.

quiz.q: At deuce, each point is a 50–50 coin flip. What's the chance the next two points end back at deuce?
quiz.hint: List all four ways two points can go: WW, WL, LW, LL.
quiz.why: WL and LW both lead back to deuce, and each has a 25% chance, so 50%.

quiz.q: Federer won about 80% of his matches. About what share of points did he win?
quiz.hint: Remember the ladder: a small edge at the bottom becomes big at the top.
quiz.why: Because scoring stacks layers, a 54% edge on points grew into about 80% of matches.

page.think: If you could change one rule of tennis scoring, would upsets become more or less common? Why?
